title: Contract improvement
audience: Supervisors and account leads who review service records and propose improvements to a contract.
learningOutcomes: Review service records to find the areas where the contract and the work do not match.
Propose a change to scope, frequency or method in writing, with the reasons.
Refrain from promising changes until the contract owner has approved them.

instruction.heading: Reviewing the record
instruction.body: Review the visit records, the checklists, the client feedback, the complaint log and, where kept, the time records, to see where the contract and the work do not match. A recurring complaint, a repeated missed item, or an area that always takes more time than the scope allows is a sign that the scope, the frequency or the method may need to change. Start with a defined period, such as the last few months of visits, and count what happened in it. Separate one-off events from patterns. A single bad visit is not evidence of a scope problem, but the same item missed across several visits is. Note the conditions that may explain the pattern, such as a season, a staffing change, a building works period or a new product, so that the proposal does not blame the team. Use the record, not impressions, and mark any gaps in the record so that they are not filled by guesswork.

instruction.heading: Building the evidence
instruction.body: For each proposed change, build a short evidence summary. It should state the source records and their dates, the count or frequency of the event, the time or product it consumes, and any conditions that affect it. Where time is measured, compare the planned time with the recorded time. For example, a bathroom planned at a set time that routinely takes longer may need its time reviewed, but the figures in your proposal must come from your own records. Do not use invented figures in a proposal. If an example figure is needed to explain a calculation, label it clearly as an example. Be careful to separate routine cleaning from work that is outside routine cleaning. Removing growth from a surface, repairing a leak, or replacing a damaged fitting is not part of routine cleaning and should be referred to the appropriate person.

instruction.heading: Writing the proposal
instruction.body: Write the proposal in plain, factual language. Include the current scope, the observed mismatch, the evidence summary, the proposed change to scope, frequency or method, the time and product implications, what the client would gain, and any limits or risks. Include an option to keep the current arrangement and monitor the result, where that is reasonable. The proposal is not a promise and does not change the contract. Send it to the contract owner for a decision. Do not include a new price unless the pricing rules for the contract allow you to propose one, and label any price as a proposal for approval.

instruction.heading: Approval and follow-up
instruction.body: The contract owner decides. Do not start the changed work, promise a new frequency, or quote a new price until the change has been approved in writing and recorded. A forward-looking promise about frequency or price is a claim about future performance, and the ACCC's guidance says that such claims need reasonable grounds when they are made (ACCC, page dated 28 June 2026). If the change is approved, update the contract schedule, the checklist and the staff briefing, and monitor the result for the period agreed in the approval. Report back on the monitoring. If the change is refused, record the decision and revisit only when new evidence is available.

instruction.heading: Where the proposal meets remediation
instruction.body: Some records describe a problem that cleaning cannot fix. Mould is a useful example. SafeWork NSW guidance says that investigating mould can be difficult and is in some cases best left to an experienced professional. It also says that where the source of growth is unclear and people may be at risk, sampling should be carried out by a competent person with suitable equipment and PPE, and that cleaning starts by fixing the moisture or ventilation problem, because mould returns otherwise (SafeWork NSW, modified 4 December 2025). A proposal that asks for more frequent cleaning of a mould-prone area without addressing the moisture source is not a fix. Refer the underlying problem, and propose only the cleaning scope that remains after the referral.

procedure: Review visit records, checklists, feedback and complaint logs for mismatches between the contract and the work, over a defined period.
Separate one-off events from patterns, and note the conditions that may explain each pattern.
Build an evidence summary for each proposed change, with sources, counts, time and product implications.
Refer any problem that is outside routine cleaning, such as growth requiring investigation or a building fault, to the appropriate person.
Write the proposal with the scope, time and product implications, the benefits, the limits and the options.
Send the proposal to the contract owner, and do not start or promise the change until it is approved in writing.

workedExamples.situation: The records show that a bathroom always needs extra time for mould-prone grout, which the contract does not account for, and the mould returns between visits.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you propose, and what do you refer?
workedExamples.reasoning: Build the evidence summary from the visit records, with the dates and the recorded extra time. Note that growth needing investigation, and any moisture source, are outside routine cleaning and may need a competent person. Refer the moisture or ventilation question to the site. Propose only the cleaning scope that remains after referral, such as a checklist change or an agreed frequency, with the time and product implications. Send it to the contract owner and do not promise the change.

workedExamples.situation: A window ledge is listed as missed in several of the most recent visits, and the contract includes the ledge in the scope.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is this a scope change, and what should the proposal say?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contract already includes the item, so the problem is most likely the method, the checklist or the time allowed, not the scope. Check the visit records and the training records first. If the item is repeatedly missed because the checklist is unclear, propose a checklist change in writing, with the evidence. Do not propose a price change until the cause is known.

workedExamples.situation: A client complains about a single visit and asks for a change of frequency, but the visit records for the other months look normal.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should a change be proposed now?
workedExamples.reasoning: One complaint without a pattern is not enough evidence for a change of frequency. Record the complaint, check the visit that it refers to, and tell the contract owner what the records show. Continue recording over the agreed period. If a pattern appears, build the evidence summary and propose the change then.

equipmentAndPpe: Visit records, checklists, feedback and complaint logs.
Time records for recurring tasks, where kept.
Proposal template with fields for scope, evidence, time, product, benefits and limits.
Copy of the current contract and schedule.
PPE for any site visit is set by the site and the task risk assessment. No PPE is required for the desk review.

commonErrors.error: Starting a change before it is approved.
commonErrors.prevention: Propose the change, then wait for the approval in writing.

commonErrors.error: Proposing a change from impression alone.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the records as evidence, and label any example figure.

commonErrors.error: Promising a new price or frequency.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave pricing and frequency to the contract owner.

commonErrors.error: Treating investigation or remediation as routine cleaning.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer growth needing investigation and any moisture source to the appropriate person.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Mould at work (NSW): SafeWork NSW guidance says mould investigation is in some cases best left to an experienced professional, that sampling where the source is unclear and people may be at risk should be carried out by a competent person with suitable equipment and PPE, and that cleaning starts by fixing the moisture or ventilation problem. The page was published 23 July 2025 and modified 4 December 2025 (NSW only).
This lesson does not authorise remediation work of any kind, and it does not grant any licence or qualification.

Forward-looking claims: the ACCC states that predictions about future matters need reasonable grounds at the time the claim is made (ACCC, page dated 28 June 2026). A proposal is not a claim to a client until it is approved and the contract is changed.

qualityStandard: Mismatch identified from sample visit records in the desk exercise, with the source records and dates listed.
Proposal written with evidence, time and product implications, limits and options, and not started or promised, in the case study.
Referral made for any item outside routine cleaning, in the case study.
Approval decision recorded before any change is started.
documentationEvidence: Evidence summary from visit records, with dates, counts and the source of each figure.
Written change proposal, with any example figure labelled as an example.
Referral record for any item outside routine cleaning.
Approval or refusal record, and the monitoring note after any approved change.
summary: Review the records to find mismatches, and separate one-off events from patterns.
Propose changes in writing, with evidence and the time and product implications.
Refer problems that are outside routine cleaning, such as growth needing investigation.
Do not start or promise a change until it is approved in writing.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a proposal to change scope be based on?
options: The client's mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: When can a change be started?
options: Once you have proposed it to the client in writing
Once approved in writing by the contract owner
Once the cleaner decides it is better

knowledgeChecks.question: A recurring extra-time item is found in the records. What is correct?
options: Stop doing the item without telling anyone
Propose a change in writing with the evidence
